Reference: Aronoff and Rafey (2026)

Model Setting

The paper builds an empirical framework for valuing environmental offset markets and applies it to Florida wetlands. Under the Clean Water Act and the 1972 Florida Water Resources Act, regulators enforce a No Net Loss rule: a landowner may develop a protected wetland only if the loss is offset by an equal gain elsewhere in the same hydrological region. Since the Florida banking rules of 1994, the offsets are produced by wetland mitigation banks, long-lived firms that place private land under a permanent conservation easement, restore or create wetlands, and receive certified offset credits from the regulator over time as restoration is verified. Developers buy credits bilaterally (often through brokers) from banks located in the same service area, a market boundary that approximates a hydrological region. The regulator converts wetland attributes into credits with a uniform assessment method that captures ecological and hydrological functions, but it does not account for the flood protection that wetlands provide to nearby property.

The new data cover 1995-2018: an administrative ledger of all state offset transactions, contracts and release schedules for every bank, transaction prices from a private broker and public-records requests, 30-m NOAA C-CAP land cover maps for 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016, public land ownership, and FEMA flood insurance claims, policies and flood hazard maps, all matched to 1,378 local watersheds (1,004 inside offset markets). Five facts motivate the model. Cumulative sales were about 1.1 billion dollars (2020 dollars), growing about 9.8% per year. Markets are concentrated: fewer than three banks trade in an average market, the median bank produces about 200 credits over its life while the median developer buys 1.1 credits, and the average bank owns 26.1% of its market's production potential. Banks take time to build: the regulator typically releases 15% of a bank's credits every 3 years, about 18.2 years for a full project, and the median bank holds 52% of its credits in reserve. Prices (about 88,000 dollars per credit) exceed observed bank costs (about 24,000 dollars per credit). Finally, trade relocates wetlands from densely developed, flood-exposed cores to peripheral watersheds near public conservation land.

The model has three blocks: (1) many small, myopic landowners decide each period whether to develop their wetland, which requires buying credits at the market price (offset demand); (2) a few large banks enter by paying a sunk cost, receive credits on a fixed release schedule, and sell them over time in a dynamic oligopoly with storage (offset supply); (3) flood damages in each watershed depend on wetlands lost to development and wetlands restored by banks. Gains from trade are measured relative to the pre-market benchmark of direct conservation, under which the wetlands that were developed would have been conserved and the banks would not have entered.

Location iii holds a wetland at time ttt if wit=1w_{it}=1wit​=1 and not if wit=0w_{it}=0wit​=0; time is discrete with an infinite horizon and discount factor δ<1\delta<1δ<1. Offset Supply

Supply is a dynamic oligopoly among a finite set of potential production sites f∈{1,2,…,F}f\in\{1,2,\ldots,F\}f∈{1,2,…,F}, each a subset If⊂[0,1]I_f\subset[0,1]If​⊂[0,1] of positive measure with wi0=0w_{i0}=0wi0​=0, differing in restoration suitability and lifetime production potential υ~f\tilde{\upsilon}_fυ~f​. In each period one potential entrant arrives at a random unoccupied site, observes υ~f\tilde{\upsilon}_fυ~f​, and draws a private entry cost

κft∼Gt(⋅∣υ~f,Ftc)(9.4.1.4)\kappa_{ft}\sim G_t\left(\cdot\mid\tilde{\upsilon}_f,\mathcal{F}_t^c\right) \tag{9.4.1.4}κft​∼Gt​(⋅∣υ~f​,Ftc​)(9.4.1.4)

where Ftc\mathcal{F}_t^cFtc​ collects observable characteristics of the remaining production sites. The fixed cost includes permitting, restoration, maintenance and the opportunity cost of nonwetland use (and possibly a warm glow from conservation). Entry is irreversible; an entrant who declines disappears, as in Doraszelski and Satterthwaite (2010).

Because verification is gradual, the regulator issues credits according to the bank's age TftT_{ft}Tft​, a release schedule

bft=B(Tft,υ~f)(9.4.1.5)b_{ft}=\mathcal{B}(T_{ft},\tilde{\upsilon}_f) \tag{9.4.1.5}bft​=B(Tft​,υ~f​)(9.4.1.5)

Restoration costs are paid up front, so the marginal cost of producing and selling credits is zero. Each incumbent holds a stock Bft≥0B_{ft}\geq 0Bft​≥0 of certified but unsold credits and chooses sales qft≤Bftq_{ft}\leq B_{ft}qft​≤Bft​. Sales jointly determine the price vector through (inverted) demand, and

with Bft=0B_{ft}=0Bft​=0 before entry. This credit inventory is what makes trading dynamic.

Estimation: Offset Demand

Demand is estimated at the watershed-by-period level (HUC12 watersheds; periods 1996-2001, 2001-2006, 2006-2011, 2011-2016). The observed development share ωht=Qht/Wht\omega_{ht}=Q_{ht}/W_{ht}ωht​=Qht​/Wht​, where QhtQ_{ht}Qht​ is private wetland area developed in hhh during ttt, is treated as the logit choice probability, giving the inversion

ln⁡ωht−ln⁡(1−ωht)=θ′Xht+θPυ~hPht+ξht(9.4.1.12)\ln\omega_{ht}-\ln(1-\omega_{ht})=\theta'X_{ht}+\theta_P\tilde{\upsilon}_hP_{ht}+\xi_{ht} \tag{9.4.1.12}lnωht​−ln(1−ωht​)=θ′Xht​+θP​υ~h​Pht​+ξht​(9.4.1.12)

where PhtP_{ht}Pht​ is the average credit price and XhtX_{ht}Xht​ includes period and water district fixed effects, flood zone shares, development on nonwetlands, lagged development density and lagged demographics (population, median income). Note that the price term enters this estimating equation with a plus sign, so the estimated θP\theta_PθP​ is negative; in the behavioral equation above it is written with a minus sign. The rest of the paper uses the estimated sign.

Identification: Offset Demand

Prices respond to banks' beliefs about ξht\xi_{ht}ξht​, so price is endogenous. Three sets of supply-side cost shifters serve as instruments. (1) Historical sunk capacity: average capacity of past entrants whose service areas contain hhh. Capacity is fixed at entry and cannot be revised, so conditional on information known at entry it is an excluded shifter of future costs (Berry and Compiani (2023)); slow release (about 18 years) keeps it relevant. The threat is that entrants had private information on future demand shocks; bankers report forecasting from public information. (2) Hausman (1996) instruments: prices and historical entrant capacity in other markets of the same water district. (3) Public wetland and conservation land in other watersheds of the same market, which shifts restoration costs through land availability and connectivity, with some time variation from the Florida Forever and Preservation 2000 buyback programs. All three lower prices as theory predicts.

Estimation: Restoration Costs

Supply is estimated in two steps following Bajari, Benkard and Levin (2007): first estimate entry, trading and production policies; then forward-simulate value functions and invert the entry condition to recover the cost distribution. Banks may enter some markets because costs are low, because entry is profitable, or both; conditional on simulated payoffs, residual variation in entry identifies fixed costs. To avoid the curse of dimensionality, policies depend on an approximate market state s^t≡{t,∑hWht,∑hWhtpublic,∑hXht,∣Ft∣,∑fBft}\hat{s}_t\equiv\{t,\sum_hW_{ht},\sum_hW_{ht}^{public},\sum_hX_{ht},|\mathcal{F}_t|,\sum_fB_{ft}\}s^t​≡{t,∑h​Wht​,∑h​Whtpublic​,∑h​Xht​,∣Ft​∣,∑f​Bft​}: year, total private and public wetland, total population, income, flood risk and water district, number of incumbents ∣Ft∣|\mathcal{F}_t|∣Ft​∣, and total reserves. Market-year entry is a probit

with Φ\PhiΦ the Gaussian CDF and ggg log-linear. Entry is more frequent in markets with more wetlands, more developed land, more nonwetland development and fewer incumbents.

Flood damages DhD_hDh​ follow a conditional Poisson process. Development QhtQ_{ht}Qht​ and bank restoration BhtB_{ht}Bht​ are allowed to have asymmetric effects (impervious surfaces versus restored function), with marginal effects proportional to underlying risk D\mathcal{D}D:

The Poisson quasi-MLE specification, using average annual 2016-2020 claims on structures built before 1995 (to capture spillovers rather than new exposed buildings) and controlling for 1991-1995 claims, is

E[claimsh,post]=exp⁡(ζdln⁡Qh,1996−2016+ζb⋅asinh⁡Bh,1996−2016+φ(claimsh,pre)+γ′Xh)(9.4.1.18)\mathbb{E}[claims_{h,post}]=\exp\left(\zeta_d\ln Q_{h,1996-2016}+\zeta_b\cdot\operatorname{asinh}B_{h,1996-2016}+\varphi(claims_{h,pre})+\gamma'X_h\right) \tag{9.4.1.18}E[claimsh,post​]=exp(ζd​lnQh,1996−2016​+ζb​⋅asinhBh,1996−2016​+φ(claimsh,pre​)+γ′Xh​)(9.4.1.18)

with ζ=(ζd,ζb)\zeta=(\zeta_d,\zeta_b)ζ=(ζd​,ζb​), φ(x)≡ρ01x>0+ρ1x+ρ2x2\varphi(x)\equiv\rho_0\mathbf{1}_{x>0}+\rho_1x+\rho_2x^2φ(x)≡ρ0​1x>0​+ρ1​x+ρ2​x2, and XhX_hXh​ including nonwetland development, shares in flood zones A and V, baseline development densities and water district fixed effects. The exponential mean fits claims that span eight orders of magnitude, and Poisson qMLE is robust to distributional misspecification. Identification relies on selection on observables: historical claims, prior development, flood hazard maps and contemporaneous nonwetland development absorb shocks that drive both wetland loss and flood exposure. Upstream and downstream spillovers are tested and found irrelevant, so the watershed is the unit of analysis.

Key Estimates

  • Demand: OLS gives θP=−0.34\theta_P=-0.34θP​=−0.34 (average elasticity about -0.3). IV estimates imply elasticities close to -1; the preferred column with sunk capacity and lagged demographics gives θ^P=−0.98\hat{\theta}_P=-0.98θ^P​=−0.98 (s.e. 0.26, scaled by 1/100,000), an average elasticity of -0.85 (s.d. 0.44), first-stage F=117.3F=117.3F=117.3, and aggregate consumer surplus of 1.67 billion dollars. First-stage FFF ranges from 49.8 to 117.3 for sunk capacity, 8.3 for Hausman and 21.3 for public land.

  • Bank costs: entry probabilities average 0.12 per market-year. Realized entry costs average 8.4 million dollars per bank, or 29,000 dollars per credit (median 13,700; IQR 5,800-35,500), close to contract costs not used in estimation (5.3 million per bank, 24,000 per credit). The implied return on capital averages 6.1% (IQR 1.8-8.3%), similar to the 5.86% real return on US housing. Unconditional costs are much higher than realized ones, showing strong selection into banking.

  • Floods: controlling for historical claims, ζ^d=0.245\hat{\zeta}_d=0.245ζ^​d​=0.245 (about half the naive 0.428) and ζ^b=−0.093\hat{\zeta}_b=-0.093ζ^​b​=−0.093; 10 percentage points more storm-surge zone raises expected damages by 29.2%. Annual damage spillovers from developing wetlands average about 1,400 dollars per hectare and 25,200 dollars per hectare in storm-surge zones, more than an order of magnitude below what Taylor and Druckenmiller (2022) would imply for Florida.

Welfare: Gains from Trade

Private gains from trade equal developer values minus bank fixed costs, integrated over observed trades, relative to direct conservation. Developer surplus in hhh and ttt follows Small and Rosen (1981):

U^ht=∫εmax⁡{u(Xht,ξht;θ^)−υ~hPht+ε1,ε0}dFε=1υ~hθ^Pln⁡(1+exp⁡{θ^′Xht−υ~hθ^PPht+ξ^ht})(9.4.1.19)\begin{aligned} \hat{U}_{ht}&=\int_\varepsilon\max\left\{u(X_{ht},\xi_{ht};\hat{\theta})-\tilde{\upsilon}_hP_{ht}+\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_0\right\}dF_\varepsilon\\ &=\frac{1}{\tilde{\upsilon}_h\hat{\theta}_P}\ln\left(1+\exp\left\{\hat{\theta}'X_{ht}-\tilde{\upsilon}_h\hat{\theta}_PP_{ht}+\hat{\xi}_{ht}\right\}\right) \end{aligned} \tag{9.4.1.19}U^ht​​=∫ε​max{u(Xht​,ξht​;θ^)−υ~h​Pht​+ε1​,ε0​}dFε​=υ~h​θ^P​1​ln(1+exp{θ^′Xht​−υ~h​θ^P​Pht​+ξ^​ht​})​(9.4.1.19)

aggregated over private wetlands in market mmm into CSm=∑t∑h∈mυ~hWhtU^htCS_m=\sum_t\sum_{h\in m}\tilde{\upsilon}_hW_{ht}\hat{U}_{ht}CSm​=∑t​∑h∈m​υ~h​Wht​U^ht​. The realized cost of each entrant is the conditional mean of the cost draw given entry,

κ^f=E[κ∣entryf=1,xf]=1G(V^f)⋅∫−∞V^fk dG(k∣xf)(9.4.1.20)\hat{\kappa}_f=\mathbb{E}[\kappa\mid entry_f=1,x_f]=\frac{1}{G(\hat{V}_f)}\cdot\int_{-\infty}^{\hat{V}_f}k\,dG(k\mid x_f) \tag{9.4.1.20}κ^f​=E[κ∣entryf​=1,xf​]=G(V^f​)1​⋅∫−∞V^f​​kdG(k∣xf​)(9.4.1.20)

and producer surplus PSmPS_mPSm​ is built from ∑f∈m(V^f−κ^f)\sum_{f\in m}(\hat{V}_f-\hat{\kappa}_f)∑f∈m​(V^f​−κ^f​) through an aggregate marginal producer surplus curve integrated over observed trades (banks have unsold credits at the end of the sample). Following Rafey (2023), welfare integrates estimated value functions over observed trade flows instead of solving a new equilibrium. The private gains from trade and net welfare (gains minus flood externalities FDFDFD, stated in words in the paper) are

GFTm=CSm+PSm,Welfare=∑mGFTm−FD(9.4.1.21)GFT_m=CS_m+PS_m,\qquad Welfare=\sum_mGFT_m-FD \tag{9.4.1.21}GFTm​=CSm​+PSm​,Welfare=m∑​GFTm​−FD(9.4.1.21)

Developer values total about 2.85 billion dollars and supply costs about 440 million, so private gains from trade are 2.41 billion dollars (2020 dollars, 1995-2020): consumer surplus 1.68 billion and producer surplus 732 million. The large gains reflect marginal opportunity costs of conservation well above the cost of producing new wetlands.

Welfare: Flood Externalities

Development is irreversible, so the social cost of lost flood protection is a perpetuity of annual marginal damages implied by the flood damage function, discounted at a 5% real rate (federal guidelines), with 3% and 7% as alternatives. Writing MDhMD_hMDh​ for the annual marginal damage per credit in hhh (this formula is written in words in the paper), the externality per credit is Eh=∑t=0∞0.95t MDhE_h=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}0.95^t\,MD_hEh​=∑t=0∞​0.95tMDh​. The hydrological externality is extremely heterogeneous: about 6,600 dollars per credit in a first-tercile watershed (negligible relative to an 88,000 dollar price), but 792,000 dollars and 1.6 million dollars per credit at the 90th and 95th percentiles, above observed prices. Wetlands lost to offset trade during 1996-2016 would have delivered 1.7-1.9 billion dollars of flood protection; the baseline flood damage is 1,888 million dollars (1,133 million at 7% and 2,643 million at 3%), so market welfare relative to direct conservation is only 522 million dollars. Damages arise because flood protection is positively correlated with the opportunity cost of conservation and uncorrelated with where banks choose to locate.

Counterfactuals

Solving a new dynamic oligopoly equilibrium is infeasible, so counterfactuals are benchmarks that hold the set of incumbent banks fixed, keep the estimated trading policies where the caps do not bind, and recompute the myopic Cournot caps under the new demand. The main reform is a locally differentiated Pigouvian tax: developers in hhh pay a tax per credit τh\tau_hτh​ equal to the expected marginal damage of observed development in their watershed, and bank sales in market mmm are subsidized in proportion to average expected flood protection from banks there. The developer's decision rule becomes (an explicit restatement of the reform described in words)

u(Xht,ξht;θ)−υ~hθP(Pt+τh)+ϵit1−ϵit0≥0(9.4.1.22)u(X_{ht},\xi_{ht};\theta)-\tilde{\upsilon}_h\theta_P(P_t+\tau_h)+\epsilon_{it1}-\epsilon_{it0}\geq 0 \tag{9.4.1.22}u(Xht​,ξht​;θ)−υ~h​θP​(Pt​+τh​)+ϵit1​−ϵit0​≥0(9.4.1.22)

The reform keeps No Net Loss and can be implemented by prices or quantities on either side.

  • Pigouvian tax: development falls from 141,606 to 120,098 acres, private gains fall from 2,410 to 2,065 million dollars, flood damage falls from 1,888 to 282 million (more than 80% of damages, or 1.6 billion dollars, avoided), and welfare rises from 522 to 1,783 million. Each dollar of forgone gains buys more than 4 dollars of flood protection, (1,888−282)/(2,410−2,065)=1606/345=4.66(1{,}888-282)/(2{,}410-2{,}065)=1606/345=4.66(1,888−282)/(2,410−2,065)=1606/345=4.66. Tax revenue is 185 million; returning it lump sum to banks cuts the producer surplus loss from 26% to about 1%.

  • Uniform tax: the welfare-maximizing Florida-wide tax is 97,000 dollars per credit (about the mean price). It cuts development to 75,169 acres and damages to 715 million, but private gains fall to 1,831 million and welfare is 1,117 million, about half the gain of the local design.

  • Market structure: with full passthrough avoided damages are 103% and welfare gains 96% of the benchmark; banks expand supply under the reform, lowering producer prices by 3.9% (consumer passthrough 78.8%). Under myopic Cournot prices fall 6.2% (passthrough 70.3%), under myopic collusion passthrough is 99.8% because of logit curvature. Banks capture 46% of gains if they collude versus 26-30% otherwise. Flood benefits equal 127-159% of the welfare gain and 2.7-4.6 times the forgone private gains, so compensating transfers could make the reform a Pareto improvement.

Extensions

Several caveats bound the results. Developers are myopic and act independently, so strategic delay and coordinated multi-parcel projects are ruled out. Counterfactuals hold entry fixed and do not let banks update beliefs over future states, so lower entry under weaker demand is not captured. Flood damages use insured claims only, ignoring uninsured losses, losses above policy limits and defensive investment. Welfare assumes lawful implementation of No Net Loss for nonflood wetland functions. Alternative designs include removing very high-risk watersheds from service areas or local permit denials. The framework applies to other offset markets where production differs from abatement, suppliers are concentrated, verification takes years, or some environmental dimensions are left out of trading rules.

The first line is a definition and the second is the regulatory constraint. The indicator wit∈{0,1}w_{it}\in\{0,1\}wit​∈{0,1} says whether location iii is a wetland at time ttt, and υ~i\tilde{\upsilon}_iυ~i​ is the number of offset credits the regulator's uniform assessment method assigns to that location, a scalar summary of the attribute vector υi∈V\upsilon_i\in\mathcal{V}υi​∈V. Integrating over the unit continuum of locations gives the aggregate regulatory wetland value υ~(wt)\tilde{\upsilon}(w_t)υ~(wt​), measured in credits. No Net Loss requires this aggregate never to fall below its initial level.

The constraint is on a sum, not on each location, and this is what creates room for trade. Taking the difference between dates ttt and 000 and using the fact that development and restoration are absorbing,

This is a primitive of the supply side: the sunk cost κft\kappa_{ft}κft​ that the potential entrant arriving at site fff in period ttt must pay to become a bank is a random draw, private information of that entrant, from a conditional distribution GtG_tGt​. It is measured in dollars per bank and bundles permitting, restoration and construction, long-term maintenance, and the opportunity cost of giving up nonwetland use of the land forever; a warm glow from conservation would enter as a negative component, so the support may include low or even negative values.

The conditioning variables matter. Conditioning on υ~f\tilde{\upsilon}_fυ~f​ lets larger projects cost more in total (and allows scale economies per credit); conditioning on Ftc\mathcal{F}_t^cFtc​, the characteristics of the sites that remain unoccupied, lets costs rise as the best sites are taken; the subscript ttt allows shifts over time. Because the draw is private and i.i.d. across entrants given these observables, rivals and the econometrician face a smooth entry probability, equation (10), instead of a deterministic entry rule, which is what guarantees existence of equilibrium in pure strategies and makes entry estimable as a binary choice in equation (13).

The distribution is not assumed known. It is recovered in the second estimation step by matching the estimated entry probability to GtG_tGt​ evaluated at the simulated value of entry, equation (16), and it delivers the realized cost of each observed entrant in equation (20).

The release schedule is a deterministic rule of the regulator, not a choice of the bank. A bank of age TftT_{ft}Tft​ with lifetime capacity υ~f\tilde{\upsilon}_fυ~f​ receives bftb_{ft}bft​ newly certified credits in period ttt, and the flows add up to capacity,

∑tbft=υ~f\sum_{t}b_{ft}=\tilde{\upsilon}_ft∑​bft​=υ~f​

The function B\mathcal{B}B captures time to build: restoration has to be verified in stages before credits can be sold, so a bank cannot bring its full capacity to market at entry. In the data a typical release is 15 percent of capacity every three years.

Three modeling consequences follow. First, since capacity and the schedule are fixed in the initial contract and restoration is paid up front, the marginal cost of a credit is zero and the only supply decisions are entry and the timing of sales. Second, bftb_{ft}bft​ is the inflow in the inventory law of motion in equation (6), so the schedule is an exogenous capacity constraint that binds for young banks and relaxes with age; this is why age TftT_{ft}Tft​ is a state variable in equations (7) and (8). Third, because historical capacity keeps feeding the market for many years regardless of current demand shocks, past entrants' capacity is a valid supply shifter for the demand estimation in equation (12). The empirical counterpart of B\mathcal{B}B is equation (14).

The first expression is the bank's flow profit and the second is the law of motion of its inventory. Profit is revenue only, price times sales, because all restoration costs were sunk at entry and the marginal cost of selling a certified credit is zero. The price is not a parameter for the bank. Together with 0≤qft≤Bft0\leq q_{ft}\leq B_{ft}0≤qft​≤Bft​ it implies Bf,t+1≥bft≥0B_{f,t+1}\geq b_{ft}\geq 0Bf,t+1​≥bft​≥0. Iterating from entry, where the stock is zero,

Bf,t+1=∑s≤tbfs−∑s≤tqfsB_{f,t+1}=\sum_{s\leq t}b_{fs}-\sum_{s\leq t}q_{fs}Bf,t+1​=s≤t∑​bfs​−s≤t∑​qfs​

so cumulative sales can never exceed cumulative releases, and lifetime sales are bounded by υ~f\tilde{\upsilon}_fυ~f​. Storage is what makes the trading problem dynamic: a credit not sold today can be sold later, so the opportunity cost of a sale is the discounted shadow value of a credit in inventory, as formalized in equation (8).

The state sts_tst​ lists everything that is payoff relevant and commonly observed at the start of period ttt. The demand block is (Wt,Xt,ξt)(W_t,X_t,\xi_t)(Wt​,Xt​,ξt​): the remaining private wetland stocks by watershed, the observed shifters and the unobserved shocks, which together with a price determine demand through equation (3). The supply block has two parts: Ftc\mathcal{F}_t^cFtc​, the characteristics of sites still available to entrants, which governs the entry cost distribution in equation (4) and future competition; and, for each incumbent f∈Ftf\in\mathcal{F}_tf∈Ft​, its capacity υ~f\tilde{\upsilon}_fυ~f​, inventory BftB_{ft}Bft​ and age TftT_{ft}Tft​, which determine how much each rival can sell now and will be able to sell later through equations (5) and (6).

Restricting strategies to depend on history only through sts_tst​ is the Markov perfect equilibrium refinement; anonymity and symmetry mean a bank's policy depends on its own (B,T,υ~f)(B,T,\tilde{\upsilon}_f)(B,T,υ~f​) and on the distribution of rivals' states, not on their identities. The state has endogenous components (WtW_tWt​, the inventories, ages, the set of incumbents) and exogenous ones (Xt,ξtX_t,\xi_tXt​,ξt​, which follow the Markov process HX,ξH_{X,\xi}HX,ξ​).

The object is very high dimensional, since it contains a vector of wetland stocks and a triple for every incumbent. This is why the equilibrium is never solved and why estimation replaces sts_tst​ by the low-dimensional aggregate s^t\hat{s}_ts^t​ in equations (13), (15) and the trading policy, an approximation in the spirit of moment-based or oblivious equilibrium concepts.

Start from the incumbent's sequential problem. Taking rivals' Markov strategies and the entry process as given, bank fff with inventory BBB and age TTT chooses a contingent plan of sales to maximize expected discounted revenue subject to the inventory constraint and law of motion in equation (6):

V(B,T,st,υ~f)=max⁡{qf,t+j}j≥0Et[∑j=0∞δjΠ(qf,t+j,st+j)]s.t. 0≤qf,t+j≤Bf,t+j,  Bf,t+j+1=Bf,t+j−qf,t+j+bf,t+jV(B,T,s_t,\tilde{\upsilon}_f)=\max_{\{q_{f,t+j}\}_{j\geq 0}}\mathbb{E}_t\left[\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\delta^j\Pi(q_{f,t+j},s_{t+j})\right]\quad\text{s.t. }0\leq q_{f,t+j}\leq B_{f,t+j},\; B_{f,t+j+1}=B_{f,t+j}-q_{f,t+j}+b_{f,t+j}V(B,T,st​,υ~f​)={qf,t+j​}j≥0​max​Et​[j=0∑∞​δjΠ(qf,t+j​,st+j​)]s.t. 0≤qf,t+j​≤Bf,t+j​,Bf,t+j+1​=Bf,t+j​−qf,t+j​+bf,t+j​

Separate the first term of the sum from the rest and apply the law of iterated expectations:

V(B,T,st,υ~f)=max⁡q∈[0,B]{Π(q,st)+δ Et[max⁡{qf,t+1+j}j≥0Et+1∑j=0∞δjΠ(qf,t+1+j,st+1+j)]}V(B,T,s_t,\tilde{\upsilon}_f)=\max_{q\in[0,B]}\left\{\Pi(q,s_t)+\delta\,\mathbb{E}_t\left[\max_{\{q_{f,t+1+j}\}_{j\geq 0}}\mathbb{E}_{t+1}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\delta^j\Pi(q_{f,t+1+j},s_{t+1+j})\right]\right\}V(B,T,st​,υ~f​)=q∈[0,B]max​{Π(q,st​)+δEt​[{qf,t+1+j​}j≥0​max​Et+1​j=0∑∞​δjΠ(qf,t+1+j​,st+1+j​)]}

The inner maximization can be moved inside the expectation because the continuation plan may be contingent on st+1s_{t+1}st+1​. Because rivals play Markov strategies and (Xt,ξt)(X_t,\xi_t)(Xt​,ξt​) is first-order Markov, the continuation problem depends on the past only through next period's own state (B−q+bft,T+1)(B-q+b_{ft},T+1)(B−q+bft​,T+1), with bft=B(T,υ~f)b_{ft}=\mathcal{B}(T,\tilde{\upsilon}_f)bft​=B(T,υ~f​) from equation (5), and the market state st+1s_{t+1}st+1​. The inner maximum is therefore the same function VVV evaluated at those arguments (principle of optimality), which gives

V(B,T,st,υ~f)=max⁡q∈[0,B]Π(q,st)+δEt[V(B−q+bft,T+1,st+1,υ~f)]V(B,T,s_t,\tilde{\upsilon}_f)=\max_{q\in[0,B]}\Pi(q,s_t)+\delta\mathbb{E}_t\left[V(B-q+b_{ft},T+1,s_{t+1},\tilde{\upsilon}_f)\right]V(B,T,st​,υ~f​)=q∈[0,B]max​Π(q,st​)+δEt​[V(B−q+bft​,T+1,st+1​,υ~f​)]

The expectation is over st+1s_{t+1}st+1​ given sts_tst​ and qqq: the choice qqq affects the distribution of st+1s_{t+1}st+1​ because sales are wetland development, which lowers Wt+1W_{t+1}Wt+1​ and raises development density. At an interior optimum with a single price P(Qt,st)P(Q_t,s_t)P(Qt​,st​) the first-order condition reads

P(Qt,st)+q∂P(Qt,st)∂Q=δ Et[∂V∂B]−δ∂∂qEt[V(B′,T+1,st+1,υ~f)]B′ fixedP(Q_t,s_t)+q\frac{\partial P(Q_t,s_t)}{\partial Q}=\delta\,\mathbb{E}_t\left[\frac{\partial V}{\partial B}\right]-\delta\frac{\partial}{\partial q}\mathbb{E}_t\left[V(B',T+1,s_{t+1},\tilde{\upsilon}_f)\right]_{B'\text{ fixed}}P(Qt​,st​)+q∂Q∂P(Qt​,st​)​=δEt​[∂B∂V​]−δ∂q∂​Et​[V(B′,T+1,st+1​,υ~f​)]B′ fixed​

so marginal revenue equals the discounted shadow value of a stored credit plus the effect of today's sale on future market conditions. With zero continuation value this collapses to the static Cournot condition used in equation (15).

This equation names the solution of the Bellman problem in equation (8): Q\mathcal{Q}Q is the equilibrium trading policy, the argmax over q∈[0,Bft]q\in[0,B_{ft}]q∈[0,Bft​] evaluated at the bank's own state (Bft,Tft,υ~f)(B_{ft},T_{ft},\tilde{\upsilon}_f)(Bft​,Tft​,υ~f​) and the market state sts_tst​ of equation (7). By symmetry and anonymity the same function applies to every bank. It is in credits per period and satisfies 0≤Q≤Bft0\leq\mathcal{Q}\leq B_{ft}0≤Q≤Bft​.

What is assumed is that the maximizer is unique and that the data are generated by a single such function. Nothing else is imposed on conduct: the trading stage could look like Cournot competition, collusion, or bilateral bargaining through brokers, and the model stays agnostic. This is the logic of two-step estimators in the tradition of Bajari, Benkard and Levin: if the policy function can be estimated directly from observed sales as a function of observed states, there is no need to solve for equilibrium or to specify the stage game.

The policy is used in three places. It is approximated empirically by χ(s^t,Bft,Tft,υ~f)\chi(\hat{s}_t,B_{ft},T_{ft},\tilde{\upsilon}_f)χ(s^t​,Bft​,Tft​,υ~f​), a bounded logistic regression of sales shares capped by the static constraint in equation (15). It is plugged into the forward simulation of the value function in equation (16). And summed across incumbents it gives market supply, which must equal demand in equation (11). The cost of agnosticism is in counterfactuals: without a structural stage game the policy cannot be recomputed under a new policy regime, so counterfactuals keep the estimated χ\chiχ and only update the caps.

A potential entrant at site fff observes sts_tst​, its capacity υ~f\tilde{\upsilon}_fυ~f​ and its private cost draw κft\kappa_{ft}κft​ from equation (4). If it enters it pays κft\kappa_{ft}κft​ and becomes a bank that starts with no certified credits at age one, worth V(0,1,st,υ~f)V(0,1,s_t,\tilde{\upsilon}_f)V(0,1,st​,υ~f​) by equation (8). If it declines it disappears and gets zero. The entry payoff comparison is

V(0,1,st,υ~f)−κft⏟enterversus0⏟stay out\underbrace{V(0,1,s_t,\tilde{\upsilon}_f)-\kappa_{ft}}_{\text{enter}}\quad\text{versus}\quad\underbrace{0}_{\text{stay out}}enterV(0,1,st​,υ~f​)−κft​​​versusstay out0​​

The value of entering is strictly decreasing in κft\kappa_{ft}κft​ and the value of staying out does not depend on it, so the optimal decision is a threshold in the cost draw:

enterft=1  ⟺  κft<V(0,1,st,υ~f)enter_{ft}=1\iff\kappa_{ft}<V(0,1,s_t,\tilde{\upsilon}_f)enterft​=1⟺κft​<V(0,1,st​,υ~f​)

which is the first line. There is no option value of waiting because an entrant who declines cannot return.

For the second line, rivals and the econometrician observe sts_tst​ but not κft\kappa_{ft}κft​. The cutoff V(0,1,st,υ~f)V(0,1,s_t,\tilde{\upsilon}_f)V(0,1,st​,υ~f​) is a function of observables only, and κft\kappa_{ft}κft​ is drawn from Gt(⋅∣υ~f,Ftc)G_t(\cdot\mid\tilde{\upsilon}_f,\mathcal{F}_t^c)Gt​(⋅∣υ~f​,Ftc​) independently of everything else given those observables. Integrating the indicator over the cost distribution,

P(enterft∣st)=∫1{k<V(0,1,st,υ~f)} dGt(k∣υ~f,Ftc)=Gt(V(0,1,st,υ~f)∣υ~f,Ftc)≡ϕt(st)\begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(enter_{ft}\mid s_t)&=\int\mathbf{1}\{k<V(0,1,s_t,\tilde{\upsilon}_f)\}\,dG_t\left(k\mid\tilde{\upsilon}_f,\mathcal{F}_t^c\right)\\ &=G_t\left(V(0,1,s_t,\tilde{\upsilon}_f)\mid\tilde{\upsilon}_f,\mathcal{F}_t^c\right)\equiv\phi_t(s_t) \end{aligned}P(enterft​∣st​)​=∫1{k<V(0,1,st​,υ~f​)}dGt​(k∣υ~f​,Ftc​)=Gt​(V(0,1,st​,υ~f​)∣υ~f​,Ftc​)≡ϕt​(st​)​

If GtG_tGt​ is continuous, the weak and strict inequalities give the same probability. The formula is the basis of the cost estimates: since GtG_tGt​ is increasing, an estimate of the entry probability ϕt\phi_tϕt​ and of the value VVV pins down one point of the distribution, Gt(V)=ϕtG_t(V)=\phi_tGt​(V)=ϕt​, and variation in VVV across markets and years traces out the distribution. This is how equations (13) and (16) are combined.

The first condition is market clearing. The left side is total credits sold by incumbent banks, each following equation (9); the right side is credits demanded by developers, equation (3). Since each acre developed in hhh must be backed by υ~h\tilde{\upsilon}_hυ~h​ credits, equality of the two flows in every period is the flow form of No Net Loss in equation (1), and it is the condition that determines the price: given the sales chosen by banks, PtP_tPt​ is the price at which developers are willing to destroy exactly that many credits' worth of wetland. Summing over time and using the inventory identity in equation (6),

∑s≤tQs=∑s≤t∑fqfs≤∑s≤t∑fbfs\sum_{s\leq t}Q_s=\sum_{s\leq t}\sum_{f}q_{fs}\leq\sum_{s\leq t}\sum_{f}b_{fs}s≤t∑​Qs​=s≤t∑​f∑​qfs​≤s≤t∑​f∑​bfs​

so cumulative destruction never exceeds cumulative certified restoration.

The second condition is a transversality condition, bank by bank. The product Pt′BftP_t'B_{ft}Pt′​Bft​ is the market value of the inventory of bank fff at ttt, and the condition says its present value vanishes in the limit. It rules out paths on which a bank hoards credits forever expecting prices to grow at least as fast as the interest rate: a credit that is never sold yields no revenue, so holding a stock with positive present value in the limit cannot be optimal. It is the standard terminal condition of storage and exhaustible-resource problems, and it closes the definition of equilibrium together with the cutoff rule in equation (10) and the Bellman equation (8).

Start from the logit choice probability derived in equation (3). In watershed hhh and period ttt the fraction of the remaining private wetland stock that is developed is

ωht≡QhtWht=eδht1+eδht\omega_{ht}\equiv\frac{Q_{ht}}{W_{ht}}=\frac{e^{\delta_{ht}}}{1+e^{\delta_{ht}}}ωht​≡Wht​Qht​​=1+eδht​eδht​​

where δht\delta_{ht}δht​ is the mean index of developing and the observed share is equated with the model probability (the continuum of landowners removes sampling error). The complementary share is

1−ωht=11+eδht1-\omega_{ht}=\frac{1}{1+e^{\delta_{ht}}}1−ωht​=1+eδht​1​

Divide the first by the second, so the common denominator cancels, and take logs:

ωht1−ωht=eδht⟹ln⁡ωht−ln⁡(1−ωht)=δht\frac{\omega_{ht}}{1-\omega_{ht}}=e^{\delta_{ht}}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\ln\omega_{ht}-\ln(1-\omega_{ht})=\delta_{ht}1−ωht​ωht​​=eδht​⟹lnωht​−ln(1−ωht​)=δht​

This is the Berry inversion for a binary logit: the log odds recover the mean utility exactly, and the unobserved shock enters linearly. Finally substitute the index, with the watershed-specific average price PhtP_{ht}Pht​ in place of PtP_tPt​. In equation (3) the index is θ′Xht−υ~hθPPht+ξht\theta'X_{ht}-\tilde{\upsilon}_h\theta_PP_{ht}+\xi_{ht}θ′Xht​−υ~h​θP​Pht​+ξht​ with a positive price coefficient; the estimating equation absorbs the minus sign into the coefficient, which gives

so the θP\theta_PθP​ estimated here equals minus the θP\theta_PθP​ of equations (2) and (3) and is expected to be negative. The implied own-price elasticity of the development share follows by differentiating ln⁡ωht=δht−ln⁡(1+eδht)\ln\omega_{ht}=\delta_{ht}-\ln(1+e^{\delta_{ht}})lnωht​=δht​−ln(1+eδht​):

∂ln⁡ωht∂ln⁡Pht=θPυ~hPht(1−ωht)\frac{\partial\ln\omega_{ht}}{\partial\ln P_{ht}}=\theta_P\tilde{\upsilon}_hP_{ht}(1-\omega_{ht})∂lnPht​∂lnωht​​=θP​υ~h​Pht​(1−ωht​)

As a check, with the preferred estimate θP=−0.98\theta_P=-0.98θP​=−0.98 per 100,000 dollars, a price of 88,000 dollars, υ~h\tilde{\upsilon}_hυ~h​ close to one and a small ωht\omega_{ht}ωht​, this is about −0.98×0.88≈−0.86-0.98\times 0.88\approx-0.86−0.98×0.88≈−0.86, in line with the reported average elasticity of −0.85-0.85−0.85.

This is the first-step entry policy, a reduced-form estimate of the equilibrium entry probability ϕt(st)\phi_t(s_t)ϕt​(st​) in equation (10). The dependent variable entertenter_tentert​ equals one if a new bank enters the market in that year. The regressor is the approximate state s^t\hat{s}_ts^t​: year, total private and public wetland, aggregated demand shifters, the number of incumbents ∣Ft∣|\mathcal{F}_t|∣Ft​∣ and total reserves. The index ggg is linear in the logs of these variables and Φ\PhiΦ is the standard normal distribution function, so the model is a probit estimated on market-year observations.

It is a policy function, not a structural equation: the coefficients of ggg mix the effect of the state on the value of entry with the shape of the cost distribution, and they have no causal interpretation by themselves. Its role is to provide the left side of the inversion. Combining with equation (10),

Φ(g(s^t))=Gt(V(0,1,st,υ~f)∣υ~f,Ftc)\Phi\left(g(\hat{s}_t)\right)=G_t\left(V(0,1,s_t,\tilde{\upsilon}_f)\mid\tilde{\upsilon}_f,\mathcal{F}_t^c\right)Φ(g(s^t​))=Gt​(V(0,1,st​,υ~f​)∣υ~f​,Ftc​)

and the right side contains the value of entry, which is computed by forward simulation in equation (16). Variation in entry rates across market-years that is not explained by simulated payoffs is attributed to entry costs. A marginal effect of a state variable xxx is Φ′(g) ∂g/∂x\Phi'(g)\,\partial g/\partial xΦ′(g)∂g/∂x. The estimated signs are intuitive: more wetlands and more development (more demand) raise entry, more incumbents (more competition) lower it; the average fitted probability is 0.12 per market-year. Replacing sts_tst​ by s^t\hat{s}_ts^t​ is an approximation, and with one potential entrant per period the market-level and entrant-level probabilities coincide.

This is the empirical version of the release schedule in equation (5). The indicator 1{Tft=τ}\mathbf{1}_{\{T_{ft}=\tau\}}1{Tft​=τ}​ picks out the bank's current age, and ατ\alpha_\tauατ​ is the share of lifetime capacity υ~f\tilde{\upsilon}_fυ~f​ that the regulator certifies at age τ\tauτ. Only one term of the sum is nonzero in any period, so the equation simply says bft=αTftυ~fb_{ft}=\alpha_{T_{ft}}\tilde{\upsilon}_fbft​=αTft​​υ~f​: releases are proportional to capacity with age-specific shares. Since all credits are eventually released, the shares satisfy

∑τ≥1ατ=1,ατ≥0\sum_{\tau\geq 1}\alpha_\tau=1,\qquad\alpha_\tau\geq 0τ≥1∑​ατ​=1,ατ​≥0

Both bftb_{ft}bft​ and υ~f\tilde{\upsilon}_fυ~f​ are observed in regulatory records, so no behavioral estimation is needed. In the simulations the schedule is simplified to a uniform ten-year release,

ατ=110⋅1{τ≤10}⟹bft=υ~f10 for Tft≤10,bft=0 afterwards\alpha_\tau=\frac{1}{10}\cdot\mathbf{1}\{\tau\leq 10\}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b_{ft}=\frac{\tilde{\upsilon}_f}{10}\text{ for }T_{ft}\leq 10,\qquad b_{ft}=0\text{ afterwards}ατ​=101​⋅1{τ≤10}⟹bft​=10υ~f​​ for Tft​≤10,bft​=0 afterwards

For example, the median bank with about 200 lifetime credits receives 20 credits per year for ten years. Proportionality means a larger bank is a scaled-up copy of a smaller one in terms of timing, which rules out size-dependent verification delays. The ten-year schedule is faster than the roughly 18 years suggested by the typical contract (15 percent every three years), so it is an approximation; a faster release brings revenue forward and, other things equal, raises simulated values in equation (16) and hence the entry costs recovered from equation (10). The schedule feeds the inventory law of motion in equation (6) in every simulated path.

The cap is the sale a bank would choose if it ignored the future, that is, the static Cournot best response. Let total sales be Q=qf+∑q−ftQ=q_f+\sum q_{-ft}Q=qf​+∑q−ft​ and let P(Q,s^t)P(Q,\hat{s}_t)P(Q,s^t​) be inverse aggregate demand, obtained by inverting equation (3). With zero marginal cost, static profit from equation (6) is revenue:

max⁡qf  P(qf+∑q−ft,s^t)qf\max_{q_f}\;P\left(q_f+\sum q_{-ft},\hat{s}_t\right)q_fqf​max​P(qf​+∑q−ft​,s^t​)qf​

The first-order condition, taking rivals' sales as given, is

P(Q,s^t)+qf∂P(Q,s^t)∂Q=0P(Q,\hat{s}_t)+q_f\frac{\partial P(Q,\hat{s}_t)}{\partial Q}=0P(Q,s^t​)+qf​∂Q∂P(Q,s^t​)​=0

Divide by P(Q,s^t)>0P(Q,\hat{s}_t)>0P(Q,s^t​)>0 and multiply and divide the second term by QQQ:

1+qfQ⋅∂P(Q,s^t)∂QQP(Q,s^t)=01+\frac{q_f}{Q}\cdot\frac{\partial P(Q,\hat{s}_t)}{\partial Q}\frac{Q}{P(Q,\hat{s}_t)}=01+Qqf​​⋅∂Q∂P(Q,s^t​)​P(Q,s^t​)Q​=0

Recognize the definition η(Q,s^t)≡∂P(Q,s^t)∂QQP(Q,s^t)\eta(Q,\hat{s}_t)\equiv\frac{\partial P(Q,\hat{s}_t)}{\partial Q}\frac{Q}{P(Q,\hat{s}_t)}η(Q,s^t​)≡∂Q∂P(Q,s^t​)​P(Q,s^t​)Q​ and substitute Q=qfIR+∑q−ftQ=q_f^{IR}+\sum q_{-ft}Q=qfIR​+∑q−ft​:

1+qfIRqfIR+∑q−ft⋅η(qfIR+∑q−ft,s^t)=01+\frac{q_f^{IR}}{q_f^{IR}+\sum q_{-ft}}\cdot\eta\left(q_f^{IR}+\sum q_{-ft},\hat{s}_t\right)=01+qfIR​+∑q−ft​qfIR​​⋅η(qfIR​+∑q−ft​,s^t​)=0

Note that η\etaη is the elasticity of inverse demand (price with respect to quantity), the reciprocal of the usual price elasticity of demand, and it is negative. The condition says that at the cap the bank's market share equals −1/η-1/\eta−1/η, the absolute value of the price elasticity of demand: marginal revenue P(1+(qf/Q)η)P(1+(q_f/Q)\eta)P(1+(qf​/Q)η) is exactly zero. For a monopolist it reduces to unit elasticity.

Why this is an upper bound on dynamic sales: in the Bellman equation (8) the first-order condition sets marginal revenue equal to the discounted marginal continuation value of keeping the credit. That continuation value is nonnegative, since an extra stored credit can always be left unsold, and selling less today also preserves future demand. Hence optimal sales occur where marginal revenue is nonnegative, which means qft≤qfIRq_{ft}\leq q_f^{IR}qft​≤qfIR​ when revenue is concave in own sales. A fitted sale above the cap would lower the bank's current revenue with no future benefit, so it is truncated.

Start from the Bellman equation (8) and evaluate it at the optimum. By equation (9) the maximizer is qft=Q(st,Bft,Tft,υ~f)q_{ft}=\mathcal{Q}(s_t,B_{ft},T_{ft},\tilde{\upsilon}_f)qft​=Q(st​,Bft​,Tft​,υ~f​), so the maximum can be dropped:

V(Bft,Tft,st,υ~f)=Π(Q(st,Bft,Tft,υ~f),st)+δ Et[V(Bf,t+1,Tf,t+1,st+1,υ~f)]V(B_{ft},T_{ft},s_t,\tilde{\upsilon}_f)=\Pi\left(\mathcal{Q}(s_t,B_{ft},T_{ft},\tilde{\upsilon}_f),s_t\right)+\delta\,\mathbb{E}_t\left[V(B_{f,t+1},T_{f,t+1},s_{t+1},\tilde{\upsilon}_f)\right]V(Bft​,Tft​,st​,υ~f​)=Π(Q(st​,Bft​,Tft​,υ~f​),st​)+δEt​[V(Bf,t+1​,Tf,t+1​,st+1​,υ~f​)]

with Bf,t+1=Bft−qft+bftB_{f,t+1}=B_{ft}-q_{ft}+b_{ft}Bf,t+1​=Bft​−qft​+bft​ and Tf,t+1=Tft+1T_{f,t+1}=T_{ft}+1Tf,t+1​=Tft​+1. Write Πt∗≡Π(Q(st,Bft,Tft,υ~f),st)\Pi_t^*\equiv\Pi(\mathcal{Q}(s_t,B_{ft},T_{ft},\tilde{\upsilon}_f),s_t)Πt∗​≡Π(Q(st​,Bft​,Tft​,υ~f​),st​) for profit along the equilibrium path. Substitute the same equation for the value at t+1t+1t+1 and use the law of iterated expectations, starting from date 000:

V(Bf0,Tf0,s0,υ~f)=Π0∗+δ E0[Π1∗+δ E1[V(Bf2,Tf2,s2,υ~f)]]=Π0∗+δ E0[Π1∗]+δ2E0[V(Bf2,Tf2,s2,υ~f)]\begin{aligned} V(B_{f0},T_{f0},s_0,\tilde{\upsilon}_f)&=\Pi_0^*+\delta\,\mathbb{E}_0\left[\Pi_1^*+\delta\,\mathbb{E}_1\left[V(B_{f2},T_{f2},s_2,\tilde{\upsilon}_f)\right]\right]\\ &=\Pi_0^*+\delta\,\mathbb{E}_0\left[\Pi_1^*\right]+\delta^2\mathbb{E}_0\left[V(B_{f2},T_{f2},s_2,\tilde{\upsilon}_f)\right] \end{aligned}V(Bf0​,Tf0​,s0​,υ~f​)​=Π0∗​+δE0​[Π1∗​+δE1​[V(Bf2​,Tf2​,s2​,υ~f​)]]=Π0∗​+δE0​[Π1∗​]+δ2E0​[V(Bf2​,Tf2​,s2​,υ~f​)]​

Repeating the substitution TTT times gives

The remainder vanishes as the horizon grows: a bank can sell at most υ~f\tilde{\upsilon}_fυ~f​ credits in total, so its continuation value is bounded, and δT+1→0\delta^{T+1}\to 0δT+1→0. For T≫0T\gg 0T≫0 it is dropped.

It remains to write the expectations as integrals. so that E0[Πt∗]=∫StΠ(Q(st,Bft,Tft,υ~f),st) dHt(st∣s0)\mathbb{E}_0[\Pi_t^*]=\int_{\mathcal{S}^t}\Pi(\mathcal{Q}(s_t,B_{ft},T_{ft},\tilde{\upsilon}_f),s_t)\,dH^t(s_t\mid s_0)E0​[Πt∗​]=∫St​Π(Q(st​,Bft​,Tft​,υ~f​),st​)dHt(st​∣s0​), and therefore

In practice the integrals are computed by Monte Carlo: draw many paths of the state from the estimated transitions, entry policy (13), release schedule (14) and trading policy (capped by equation (15)), compute discounted revenue on each path, and average. These two conditions are the assumptions that pin down the functional form of the flood damage model. DhD_hDh​ is flood damage (insurance claims, in dollars per year) in watershed hhh, QhtQ_{ht}Qht​ is the wetland area developed, BhtB_{ht}Bht​ is the area restored by banks, and D(Xht,Qht,Bht)≡E[Dh∣Xht,Qht,Bht]\mathcal{D}(X_{ht},Q_{ht},B_{ht})\equiv\mathbb{E}[D_h\mid X_{ht},Q_{ht},B_{ht}]D(Xht​,Qht​,Bht​)≡E[Dh​∣Xht​,Qht​,Bht​] is the conditional mean, interpreted as underlying flood risk. Both marginal effects are proportional to D\mathcal{D}D: an acre of wetland lost matters more where expected damages are already high (dense, low-lying, storm-surge areas). Proportionality is what generates the extreme heterogeneity of the externality across watersheds.

The two effects are allowed to differ, with separate parameters ζd\zeta_dζd​ (expected positive) and ζb\zeta_bζb​ (expected negative), because paving a wetland and restoring one elsewhere are not mirror images. Dividing by D\mathcal{D}D shows what the parameters are:

∂ln⁡D∂ln⁡Qht=ζd,∂ln⁡D∂ln⁡Bht=ζbBht1+Bht2\frac{\partial\ln\mathcal{D}}{\partial\ln Q_{ht}}=\zeta_d,\qquad\frac{\partial\ln\mathcal{D}}{\partial\ln B_{ht}}=\zeta_b\frac{B_{ht}}{\sqrt{1+B_{ht}^2}}∂lnQht​∂lnD​=ζd​,∂lnBht​∂lnD​=ζb​1+Bht2​​Bht​​

So ζd\zeta_dζd​ is a constant elasticity, and the marginal damage ζdD/Qht\zeta_d\mathcal{D}/Q_{ht}ζd​D/Qht​ is decreasing in QhtQ_{ht}Qht​ when 0<ζd<10<\zeta_d<10<ζd​<1: the first acres developed do the most harm. For restoration the weight 1/1+Bht21/\sqrt{1+B_{ht}^2}1/1+Bht2​​ equals one at Bht=0B_{ht}=0Bht​=0 and behaves like 1/Bht1/B_{ht}1/Bht​ for large areas, so the elasticity rises from zero to ζb\zeta_bζb​. This form is chosen because the marginal effect stays finite when a watershed has no bank, which is the typical case; a 1/Bht1/B_{ht}1/Bht​ weight would not be defined there. Integrating these two conditions yields the estimating equation (18), and the first one, evaluated at the estimates, gives the annual marginal damage per credit MDhMD_hMDh​ used in the welfare calculations.

The specification follows from integrating the two marginal-effect conditions in equation (17). Write D=D(Xh,Qh,Bh)\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}(X_h,Q_h,B_h)D=D(Xh​,Qh​,Bh​) for the conditional mean of damages and divide each condition by D>0\mathcal{D}>0D>0:

∂ln⁡D∂Qh=ζdQh,∂ln⁡D∂Bh=ζb1+Bh2\frac{\partial\ln\mathcal{D}}{\partial Q_h}=\frac{\zeta_d}{Q_h},\qquad\frac{\partial\ln\mathcal{D}}{\partial B_h}=\frac{\zeta_b}{\sqrt{1+B_h^2}}∂Qh​∂lnD​=Qh​ζd​​,∂Bh​∂lnD​=1+Bh2​​ζb​​

Integrate the first with respect to QhQ_hQh​, holding BhB_hBh​ and XhX_hXh​ fixed; the constant of integration is a function c1c_1c1​ of the other arguments:

ln⁡D=ζdln⁡Qh+c1(Bh,Xh)\ln\mathcal{D}=\zeta_d\ln Q_h+c_1(B_h,X_h)lnD=ζd​lnQh​+c1​(Bh​,Xh​)

Differentiate this with respect to BhB_hBh​ and match the second condition, then integrate using the antiderivative of 1/1+x21/\sqrt{1+x^2}1/1+x2​, which is the inverse hyperbolic sine asinh⁡x=ln⁡(x+1+x2)\operatorname{asinh}x=\ln(x+\sqrt{1+x^2})asinhx=ln(x+1+x2​):

To verify the antiderivative, differentiate: ddxln⁡(x+1+x2)=1+x/1+x2x+1+x2=11+x2\frac{d}{dx}\ln(x+\sqrt{1+x^2})=\frac{1+x/\sqrt{1+x^2}}{x+\sqrt{1+x^2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}dxd​ln(x+1+x2​)=x+1+x2​1+x/1+x2​​=1+x2​1​. Exponentiating,

D(Xh,Qh,Bh)=exp⁡(ζdln⁡Qh+ζbasinh⁡Bh+c2(Xh))\mathcal{D}(X_h,Q_h,B_h)=\exp\left(\zeta_d\ln Q_h+\zeta_b\operatorname{asinh}B_h+c_2(X_h)\right)D(Xh​,Qh​,Bh​)=exp(ζd​lnQh​+ζb​asinhBh​+c2​(Xh​))

The remaining function c2c_2c2​ of the controls is unrestricted by equation (17). The paper parameterizes it as a flexible function of historical claims plus a linear index, c2=φ(claimsh,pre)+γ′Xhc_2=\varphi(claims_{h,pre})+\gamma'X_hc2​=φ(claimsh,pre​)+γ′Xh​ with φ(x)≡ρ01x>0+ρ1x+ρ2x2\varphi(x)\equiv\rho_0\mathbf{1}_{x>0}+\rho_1x+\rho_2x^2φ(x)≡ρ0​1x>0​+ρ1​x+ρ2​x2, and measures the outcome by post-period claims and the regressors by cumulative changes over 1996-2016:

The left side is a conditional expectation given all right-side variables. The parameters are estimated by Poisson quasi-maximum likelihood, which is consistent whenever this conditional mean is correctly specified, whatever the distribution of claims, and which keeps watersheds with zero claims. The moment conditions are ∑h(claimsh,post−exp⁡(zh′β))zh=0\sum_h(claims_{h,post}-\exp(z_h'\beta))z_h=0∑h​(claimsh,post​−exp(zh′​β))zh​=0, with zhz_hzh​ the vector of regressors and β\betaβ their coefficients. Since asinh⁡B≈ln⁡(2B)\operatorname{asinh}B\approx\ln(2B)asinhB≈ln(2B) for large BBB, ζb\zeta_bζb​ is approximately an elasticity for watersheds with sizable banks, and asinh⁡0=0\operatorname{asinh}0=0asinh0=0 handles watersheds with no bank. The term ln⁡Qh\ln Q_hlnQh​ requires positive development, so the log form applies as written only to watersheds with Qh>0Q_h>0Qh​>0. Identification is by selection on observables: conditional on historical claims, flood zones, baseline density and nonwetland development, wetland development and bank location are assumed unrelated to other determinants of claims on pre-1995 structures.

Use the behavioral sign convention of equations (2) and (3), with price coefficient θP>0\theta_P>0θP​>0, and write the mean index per acre as δht≡θ^′Xht−υ~hθ^PPht+ξ^ht\delta_{ht}\equiv\hat{\theta}'X_{ht}-\tilde{\upsilon}_h\hat{\theta}_PP_{ht}+\hat{\xi}_{ht}δht​≡θ^′Xht​−υ~h​θ^P​Pht​+ξ^​ht​. A landowner gets δht+ε1\delta_{ht}+\varepsilon_1δht​+ε1​ from developing and ε0\varepsilon_0ε0​ from not developing, both in utility units, and chooses the larger. The first step is the expected maximum. Since ε1,ε0\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_0ε1​,ε0​ are independent type 1 extreme value with distribution function exp⁡(−e−x)\exp(-e^{-x})exp(−e−x),

Pr⁡(max⁡{δht+ε1,ε0}≤x)=exp⁡(−e−(x−δht))exp⁡(−e−x)=exp⁡(−e−x(1+eδht))=exp⁡(−e−(x−ln⁡(1+eδht)))\begin{aligned} \Pr\left(\max\{\delta_{ht}+\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_0\}\leq x\right)&=\exp\left(-e^{-(x-\delta_{ht})}\right)\exp\left(-e^{-x}\right)\\ &=\exp\left(-e^{-x}\left(1+e^{\delta_{ht}}\right)\right)\\ &=\exp\left(-e^{-\left(x-\ln(1+e^{\delta_{ht}})\right)}\right) \end{aligned}Pr(max{δht​+ε1​,ε0​}≤x)​=exp(−e−(x−δht​))exp(−e−x)=exp(−e−x(1+eδht​))=exp(−e−(x−ln(1+eδht​)))​

so the maximum is again type 1 extreme value, shifted by ln⁡(1+eδht)\ln(1+e^{\delta_{ht}})ln(1+eδht​). Its mean is the shift plus Euler's constant γE≈0.577\gamma_E\approx 0.577γE​≈0.577:

∫εmax⁡{δht+ε1,ε0}dFε=ln⁡(1+eδht)+γE\int_\varepsilon\max\left\{\delta_{ht}+\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_0\right\}dF_\varepsilon=\ln\left(1+e^{\delta_{ht}}\right)+\gamma_E∫ε​max{δht​+ε1​,ε0​}dFε​=ln(1+eδht​)+γE​

The constant is the expected utility when development is impossible (δht→−∞\delta_{ht}\to-\inftyδht​→−∞), so the surplus from having the option to develop is ln⁡(1+eδht)\ln(1+e^{\delta_{ht}})ln(1+eδht​) utils per acre.

The second step converts utils into dollars per credit. One more dollar on the credit price lowers the utility of developing an acre by υ~hθ^P\tilde{\upsilon}_h\hat{\theta}_Pυ~h​θ^P​, so dividing by this number gives the money value per credit required:

U^ht=1υ~hθ^Pln⁡(1+exp⁡{θ^′Xht−υ~hθ^PPht+ξ^ht})\hat{U}_{ht}=\frac{1}{\tilde{\upsilon}_h\hat{\theta}_P}\ln\left(1+\exp\left\{\hat{\theta}'X_{ht}-\tilde{\upsilon}_h\hat{\theta}_PP_{ht}+\hat{\xi}_{ht}\right\}\right)U^ht​=υ~h​θ^P​1​ln(1+exp{θ^′Xht​−υ~h​θ^P​Pht​+ξ^​ht​})

The same expression is the Small and Rosen area under the demand curve. With development probability Λ(δ)≡eδ/(1+eδ)\Lambda(\delta)\equiv e^{\delta}/(1+e^{\delta})Λ(δ)≡eδ/(1+eδ) and a≡θ^′Xht+ξ^hta\equiv\hat{\theta}'X_{ht}+\hat{\xi}_{ht}a≡θ^′Xht​+ξ^​ht​,

∫Pht∞Λ(a−υ~hθ^Pp)dp=[−ln⁡(1+ea−υ~hθ^Pp)υ~hθ^P]Pht∞=ln⁡(1+eδht)υ~hθ^P\int_{P_{ht}}^{\infty}\Lambda\left(a-\tilde{\upsilon}_h\hat{\theta}_Pp\right)dp=\left[-\frac{\ln\left(1+e^{a-\tilde{\upsilon}_h\hat{\theta}_Pp}\right)}{\tilde{\upsilon}_h\hat{\theta}_P}\right]_{P_{ht}}^{\infty}=\frac{\ln\left(1+e^{\delta_{ht}}\right)}{\tilde{\upsilon}_h\hat{\theta}_P}∫Pht​∞​Λ(a−υ~h​θ^P​p)dp=​−υ~h​θ^P​ln(1+ea−υ~h​θ^P​p)​​Pht​∞​=υ~h​θ^P​ln(1+eδht​)​

and conversely ∂U^ht/∂Pht=−Λ(δht)\partial\hat{U}_{ht}/\partial P_{ht}=-\Lambda(\delta_{ht})∂U^ht​/∂Pht​=−Λ(δht​): a one-dollar price increase lowers expected surplus by the probability of buying. Multiplying by υ~hWht\tilde{\upsilon}_hW_{ht}υ~h​Wht​ in CSmCS_mCSm​ gives Whtln⁡(1+eδht)/θ^PW_{ht}\ln(1+e^{\delta_{ht}})/\hat{\theta}_PWht​ln(1+eδht​)/θ^P​ dollars.

Three remarks on the equation as printed. First, its first line is schematic: the integrand there is written as u−υ~hPhtu-\tilde{\upsilon}_hP_{ht}u−υ~h​Pht​ without the price coefficient, mixing utils and dollars; the second line equals the first only after the price term is multiplied by θ^P\hat{\theta}_Pθ^P​, the constant γE\gamma_EγE​ is dropped and the result is divided by υ~hθ^P\tilde{\upsilon}_h\hat{\theta}_Pυ~h​θ^P​. Second, the second line uses the positive-coefficient convention of equation (2); if the negative estimate from equation (12) is inserted, θ^P\hat{\theta}_Pθ^P​ must be replaced by its absolute value in both places, otherwise the surplus would be negative and increasing in price. Third, the formula assumes no income effects, so that the marginal utility of money is the constant θ^P\hat{\theta}_Pθ^P​.

The cost of an observed entrant is not observed, but entry reveals that the draw was below the cutoff. By the cutoff rule in equation (10), bank fff with observables xfx_fxf​ entered if and only if κ<V^f\kappa<\hat{V}_fκ<V^f​, where V^f\hat{V}_fV^f​ is the simulated value of entry from equation (16) and κ\kappaκ has distribution G(⋅∣xf)G(\cdot\mid x_f)G(⋅∣xf​) from equation (4). Pr⁡(κ≤k∣entryf=1,xf)=Pr⁡(κ≤k,  κ<V^f∣xf)Pr⁡(κ<V^f∣xf)=G(k∣xf)G(V^f∣xf)\Pr\left(\kappa\leq k\mid entry_f=1,x_f\right)=\frac{\Pr\left(\kappa\leq k,\;\kappa<\hat{V}_f\mid x_f\right)}{\Pr\left(\kappa<\hat{V}_f\mid x_f\right)}=\frac{G(k\mid x_f)}{G(\hat{V}_f\mid x_f)}Pr(κ≤k∣entryf​=1,xf​)=Pr(κ<V^f​∣xf​)Pr(κ≤k,κ<V^f​∣xf​)​=G(V^f​∣xf​)G(k∣xf​)​

and the conditional probability is one for k>V^fk>\hat{V}_fk>V^f​. This is the distribution GGG truncated from above at V^f\hat{V}_fV^f​, so its differential is dG(k∣xf)/G(V^f∣xf)dG(k\mid x_f)/G(\hat{V}_f\mid x_f)dG(k∣xf​)/G(V^f​∣xf​) on (−∞,V^f](-\infty,\hat{V}_f](−∞,V^f​]. Taking the mean,

κ^f=E[κ∣entryf=1,xf]=∫−∞V^fk dG(k∣xf)G(V^f∣xf)=1G(V^f)⋅∫−∞V^fk dG(k∣xf)\hat{\kappa}_f=\mathbb{E}[\kappa\mid entry_f=1,x_f]=\int_{-\infty}^{\hat{V}_f}k\,\frac{dG(k\mid x_f)}{G(\hat{V}_f\mid x_f)}=\frac{1}{G(\hat{V}_f)}\cdot\int_{-\infty}^{\hat{V}_f}k\,dG(k\mid x_f)κ^f​=E[κ∣entryf​=1,xf​]=∫−∞V^f​​kG(V^f​∣xf​)dG(k∣xf​)​=G(V^f​)1​⋅∫−∞V^f​​kdG(k∣xf​)

where G(V^f)G(\hat{V}_f)G(V^f​) in the note's formula is shorthand for G(V^f∣xf)G(\hat{V}_f\mid x_f)G(V^f​∣xf​), the entry probability ϕ\phiϕ of that entrant.

Two implications. Because every cost in the truncated support is below V^f\hat{V}_fV^f​, the realized cost satisfies κ^f<V^f\hat{\kappa}_f<\hat{V}_fκ^f​<V^f​ and expected producer surplus per entrant V^f−κ^f\hat{V}_f-\hat{\kappa}_fV^f​−κ^f​ is positive: entrants are selected on low costs, which is why realized costs are far below unconditional means. V^f−κ^f=1G(V^f∣xf)∫−∞V^fG(k∣xf) dk\hat{V}_f-\hat{\kappa}_f=\frac{1}{G(\hat{V}_f\mid x_f)}\int_{-\infty}^{\hat{V}_f}G(k\mid x_f)\,dkV^f​−κ^f​=G(V^f​∣xf​)1​∫−∞V^f​​G(k∣xf​)dk

As an illustration, if G(⋅∣xf)G(\cdot\mid x_f)G(⋅∣xf​) were normal with location μκ\mu_\kappaμκ​ and scale σκ\sigma_\kappaσκ​, then with zf≡(V^f−μκ)/σκz_f\equiv(\hat{V}_f-\mu_\kappa)/\sigma_\kappazf​≡(V^f​−μκ​)/σκ​ the truncated mean is

κ^f=μκ−σκΦ′(zf)Φ(zf)\hat{\kappa}_f=\mu_\kappa-\sigma_\kappa\frac{\Phi'(z_f)}{\Phi(z_f)}κ^f​=μκ​−σκ​Φ(zf​)Φ′(zf​)​

the unconditional mean minus the scale times the inverse Mills ratio. With an entry probability near 0.12, zf≈−1.17z_f\approx-1.17zf​≈−1.17 and the ratio is about 1.67, so realized costs lie well over one and a half scale units below μκ\mu_\kappaμκ​.

These are accounting definitions of the welfare measures, all relative to the benchmark of direct conservation in which no wetland is developed and no bank enters. CSm=∑t∑h∈mυ~hWhtU^htCS_m=\sum_t\sum_{h\in m}\tilde{\upsilon}_hW_{ht}\hat{U}_{ht}CSm​=∑t​∑h∈m​υ~h​Wht​U^ht​ is developer surplus in market mmm, built from equation (19): the value of being allowed to develop at the market price instead of not at all. PSmPS_mPSm​ is bank surplus, value net of realized entry cost from equations (16) and (20), prorated over observed trades because banks still hold unsold credits at the end of the sample. Their sum GFTmGFT_mGFTm​ is the private gains from trade. Payments for credits are transfers from developers to banks and cancel, so

GFTm=developer values⏟gross−bank entry costs⏟resources usedGFT_m=\underbrace{\text{developer values}}_{\text{gross}}-\underbrace{\text{bank entry costs}}_{\text{resources used}}GFTm​=grossdeveloper values​​−resources usedbank entry costs​​

All terms are present values in 2020 dollars. FDFDFD is the present value of expected flood damages caused by the wetland relocation, computed from the damage function in equations (17) and (18) as a perpetuity of marginal damages; it is an externality because neither side of the trade bears it. Net welfare subtracts it from total private gains.

The numbers: developer values of about 2.85 billion dollars minus supply costs of about 0.44 billion give gains of 2.41 billion, split into consumer surplus of 1.68 billion and producer surplus of 0.73 billion. Then

Welfare=2,410−1,888=522 million dollarsWelfare=2{,}410-1{,}888=522\text{ million dollars}Welfare=2,410−1,888=522 million dollars

so the unpriced flood externality offsets close to four fifths of the private gains. The measure excludes other unpriced wetland functions, assumed to be preserved by No Net Loss, and it integrates over observed trades without solving a new equilibrium.

This is the developer's decision rule of equation (2) under the counterfactual reform. The only change is that the developer in watershed hhh now pays Pt+τhP_t+\tau_hPt​+τh​ per credit, where τh\tau_hτh​ is a tax in dollars per credit equal to the expected marginal flood damage of development in that watershed (the present value EhE_hEh​ of the annual marginal damage MDhMD_hMDh​ implied by equation (17)). The sign convention is the behavioral one, with a positive price coefficient θP\theta_PθP​. Since the tax enters exactly like the price, the development probability keeps the logit form of equation (3) with a shifted index, and the log odds of development in equation (12) fall by the tax bill per acre in utility units:

ln⁡ωhtτ1−ωhtτ=θ′Xht−υ~hθP(Pt+τh)+ξht=ln⁡ωht1−ωht−υ~hθPτh\ln\frac{\omega_{ht}^{\tau}}{1-\omega_{ht}^{\tau}}=\theta'X_{ht}-\tilde{\upsilon}_h\theta_P(P_t+\tau_h)+\xi_{ht}=\ln\frac{\omega_{ht}}{1-\omega_{ht}}-\tilde{\upsilon}_h\theta_P\tau_hln1−ωhtτ​ωhtτ​​=θ′Xht​−υ~h​θP​(Pt​+τh​)+ξht​=ln1−ωht​ωht​​−υ~h​θP​τh​

at a given producer price PtP_tPt​. The tax is local: it is negligible in most watersheds and very large in a few flood-exposed ones, so it removes little development in total but removes the most damaging trades, which is why it outperforms a uniform tax.

The equation holds PtP_tPt​ fixed, which corresponds to full passthrough. In the market counterfactuals banks respond: lower demand tightens or relaxes the static caps of equation (15), the producer price PtP_tPt​ falls somewhat, and the consumer price rises by less than τh\tau_hτh​. Because the tax is a wedge between the price developers pay and the price banks receive, it leaves No Net Loss in equation (1) intact; welfare is then evaluated with equations (19) to (21) under the new choices. The same allocation could be implemented with watershed-specific credit requirements, that is, by scaling υ~h\tilde{\upsilon}_hυ~h​.
